sustainable and reliable tap water supply for rural households
across India. It shifts the focus from only infrastructure creation to
citizen-centric service delivery supported by strong local
governance and digital monitoring.

The move will strengthen water security, improve health outcomes
and empower rural communities, especially our Nari Shakti.

MESSAGE

Water has been revered in ourscriptures as the very source of life. As ourscriptures say, 71-1 qanete4 SM Nag Sha - May
the divine waters bringus welfare and nourishment.
The Jal Jeevan Mission has already brought about a transformative change to crores of rural households by providing
access to safe and adequate drinking water through individual household tap connections. Beyond improving the
quality of life, it has also strengthened public health outcomes and empowered India's Nari Shakti by reducing the
drudgery of fetching water from faraway sources.
Now, Jal Jeevan Mission 2.0 builds upon this strong foundation and takes this work to the next level. It establishes a
robust institutional framework for drinking water governance, complemented by digital data governance for rural
water supply systems. This phase introduces key reforms to enhance transparency, strengthen institutions and
improveservice delivery, supported by a comprehensive capacity-building framework.
Inthe true spirit of grassroots democracy, Gram Panchayats lie at the centre of this approach, envisioned as the owners
and operators of village water supply systems. With the support of digital platforms such as ‘Sujal Gaon’, they will be
better equipped to monitor, manage and maintain these systems. These tools will help connect village-level operations
with the broader water supply ecosystem, ensuring accountability from source to household.
As India advances through the Amrit Kaal towards Viksit Bharat, Jal Jeevan Mission 2.0 represents a growth from
enabling access through infrastructure creation to reliable and sustainable service delivery. This reflects our steadfast
commitment to ensuring regular water supply, assured water quality, source sustainability and efficient system
management for every household.
With continued community participation and the collective commitment of all stakeholders, Jal Jeevan Mission 2.0 will
furtherstrengthen India's journey towards a water-secure future.

(Narendra Modi)

CR Poatil FOREWORD 22™ March, 2026
Safe and reliable drinking water is the foundation ofa healthy, dignified and prosperous society. Through the Jal Jeevan
Mission, India has undertaken one of the largest transformations in rural water supply, bringing tap water to crores of
households and significantly improving the lives of millions, especially women and girls.
As we move into Jal Jeevan Mission 2.0, we are entering a new era where access to potable drinking water for every rural
household is becoming a reality. This is not merely about infrastructure; it is about ensuring a healthy and dignified life
forevery citizen.
In this phase, the focus must firmly shift to reliability of service delivery and Jan Bhagidari through GPs/ VWSCs
participation. States/ UTs must accord the highest priority to adherence to technical standards and protocols for quality
assurance. There must be regular and rigorous monitoring of works at all levels, ensuring that systems are built to last
and perform efficiently overtime.
The District Water and Sanitation Mission (DWSM) will play a central role in ensuring effective implementation and
oversight. At the same time, State Governments must put in place strong mechanisms for supervision, verification and
compliance. There must be zero tolerance for any irregularities or deviations from prescribed quality standards, as the
safety and well-being of citizens depend onit.
The introduction of Jal Utsavand a mandatory 15-daytrial period before handing overin-village infrastructure under Jal
Arpan, reflects this commitment to accountability and performance. It ensures that systems are tested, meet service
standards and deliver reliable supply before being entrusted to communities.
This has further strengthened the approach of Jal Sanchay, Jan Bhagidari & Catch the Rain Campaign in promoting
water conservation efforts. States/ UTs have been advised to take ground water recharge measures including rainwater
harvesting, borewell recharge and reuse of grey water, in convergence with schemes such as MGNREGS/ VB-G RAM Gand
SBM. These efforts will help ensure long-term sustainability of drinking water sources and reliable availability of water
for tap connections under the Mission.
At the same time, citizen accountability is at the heart of JJM 2.0. Through Jal Seva Aankalan, communities will play an
active role in assessing service delivery. These assessments will guide districts and States in preparing targeted service
improvement plans, ensuring that feedback from the ground directly shapes policy and implementation. In this way,
JJM 2.0 lays the foundation for strengthened rural drinking water governance, built on transparency, participation and
continuous improvement. ‘ ;
———
(C.R. Paatil)

V. Somanna FOREWORD 22” March, 2026
Astrong nation is built on the well-being of its people and access to safe and clean drinking water remains central to
this goal. Water has always been an integral part of India's civilisation, shaping our lives, livelihoods and traditions,
where itis respected, conserved and celebrated.
However, for many years, ensuring reliable access to safe drinking water remained a challenge in rural India, especially
for women who bore the burden of fetching water.
The launch of the Jal Jeevan Mission marked an important step in addressing this challenge. In a short span, the
Mission has made significant progress, reaching the majority of rural households and improving quality of life through
the collective efforts of States, local institutions and communities. Its impact is visible across rural India, reducing
drudgery, improving health and nutrition and strengthening community ownership.
As we move into the next phase, the focus is on sustaining these gains. Jal Jeevan Mission 2.0 marks a shift from
infrastructure creation to reliable service delivery, with Gram Panchayats and communities atthe centre.
Initiatives such as Jal Arpan and Jal Utsav are deepening Jan Bhagidari by fostering community ownership, while
Sujalam Bharat reflects a vision of transparent, technology enabled and citizen-centric water governance.
The operational guidelines for Jal Jeevan Mission 2.0 provide a clear framework to strengthen institutions, enhance
accountability and ensure long-term sustainability of rural water supply systems, supported by key structural reforms
for effective operation and maintenance.
This Guidelines will play an important role in realising water security as.a key pillar of inclusive development in India's
journey towards Viksit Bharat @2047. By ensuring universal access to safe drinking water, India is contributing to
Sustainable Development Goal 6 and demonstrating how people-led development, supported by a whole-of-
governmentand whole-of-society approach, can deliver lasting outcomes.
With this, | urge all stakeholders, States, Districts, Gram Panchayats and Citizens, to work together with a shared sense
of responsibility. Through Jan Bhagidari, we can ensure that every village not only has access to water, but also
sustains it for the future.

The Jal Jeevan Mission has brought about a significant transformation in rural water supply by expanding access to tap
water across the country. As we move into the next phase, Jal Jeevan Mission 2.0 seeks to consolidate these gains by
focusing on sustainability, efficiency and accountable service delivery.
This phase places strong emphasis on institutional reforms to strengthen drinking water governance across all levels. A
clear institutional architecture has been outlined, defining roles and responsibilities from the National to the Gram
Panchayat level, with a particular focus on empowering local institutions for effective service delivery. The District Water
and Sanitation Mission (DWSM) and District Technical Units (DTUs) will play a critical role in ensuring technical robust-
ness and implementation oversight.
At the village level, the Gram Panchayat, through its standing committee for water and sanitation (VWS5C), is positioned
at the core of service delivery. The VWSC will function as the executive arm of the Gram Panchayat, responsible for day-
to-day management, monitoring and upkeep of water supply systems. Strengthening these standing committees is
central to ensuring ownership, accountability and sustainability of services at the grassroots level.
Akey element of these reforms is the deepening of community participation. Community-based organisations such as
Self-Help Groups (SHGs) and Primary Agricultural Credit Societies (PACS) will play an active role in supporting O&M,
monitoring and local management overseen byVWSCs. This approach aims to build ownership, strengthen accountabil-
ity and ensure long-term sustainability of water supply systems.
The guidelines also emphasise digital governance and data-driven monitoring, with the use of interactive dashboards at
National, State, District and Panchayat levels. Integration with citizen interface platformssuch as Meri Panchayat Mobile
Application will enable real-time feedback, grievance redressal and participatory monitoring, thereby strengthening
transparency and responsiveness in service delivery.
These reforms also focus on strengthening technical standards, improving operational efficiency and ensuring
consistent service delivery outcomes. Together, all the measures aim to transition the sector from a scheme-based
infrastructure creation approach toa service-oriented, lifecycle-based regular water supply systems in rural india.
Jal Jeevan Mission 2.0 represents a comprehensive effort to build resilient and sustainable rural water supply systems
through strong institutions, empowered communities and effective governance mechanisms. | am confident that these
guidelines will support States, UTs in achieving the Mission's objectives and ensuring reliable drinking water services for
every rurallhousehald.

(Ashok K. K. Meena)

Kamal Kishore Soan PREFACE 22™ March, 2026
Jal Jeevan Mission has significantly improved rural drinking water access by bringing tap water within household
premises. In JJM 2.0, the focus now shifts from creating infrastructure to ensuring reliable and sustained water service
delivery. The Cabinet has approved service-delivery orientation and the guidelines reflect that direction. The heart of
JJM 2.0 is strong digital governance through the Sujalam Bharat digital framework. Every village is being assigned a
Sujal Gaon ID, mapping the entire system from source to tap. This strengthens transparency, avoids duplication and
supports better monitoring. Interactive dashboards and near real-time information flow are ensuring early flagging of
problems and quick corrections, which is very important. Command and Support Centres to ensure that projects are
built correctly and function as per plan. JJM 2.0 calls for stronger implementation systems and structural reforms.
States/ UTs to prepare and follow Comprehensive Implementation and Reform Plans (CIRP) to document road maps
forscheme completion, handing overto GPs and actions needed to keep those working.
Technical compliance remains a key requirement. Following CPHEEO norms and ensuring precise validation, States/
UTs will help in maintaining the construction quality, fair use of funds and sustainability. Decision Support Systems
(DSS) will integrate groundwater status, scheme-level data and field observations to help DWSMs plan better and act
faster, ultimately to support improved functionality. Districts are to provide technical support to GPs through District
Technical Unit (DTU), monitor progress and guide O&M practices. The idea of district-level leadership was boosted
during the 700-plus interactions with District Collectors held over last one year. Those interactions shaped the struc-
tural reforms, especially the shift towards accountability and monitoring. Initiatives like Peyjal Samvad further
strengthened the message that DWSMs must develop practical solutions, improve preventive maintenance and adopt
cost-effective practices suited to local needs. Similarly, village-level conversations like Sujal Gaon Samvad helped
communities understand their roles in keeping systems functional and reporting service gaps. As JJM 2.0 places GPs at
the centre of service delivery, schemes will be handed over through Jal Arpan, after 15 days trial run and verification to
strengthen the O&M ecosystem through Jan Bhagidari. Villagers will come together in annual Jal Utsav, as a mark to
restore commitment towards drinking water.
JJM 2.0is a step toward a stronger, transparent, community owned and managed rural water service framework. As we
begin this phase, our goal is clear: to build a service oriented, accountable and community led water supply system.
The guidelines that follow reflect the structural reforms approved by the Cabinet and outline how States/ UTs, districts
and GPs can work together to achieve this. | am confident that with collective effort, close attention to technical
standards and steady implementation of CIRP, we will ensure that every rural household receives reliable drinking
water, every day ofthe year. a aan Hiabed
(Kamal Kishore Soan)

3.3.10. SNA-SPARSH Framework and

Payment Mechanism

The SNA-SPARSH system has been envisaged as an

integrated financial framework connecting the Public

Financial Management System (PFMS), State Inte-

grated Financial Management Information System

(IFMIS) and the Reserve Bank of India’s (RBI) e-Kuber

platform. The SNA-SPARSH payment mechanism

enables NJJM to ensure just-in-time payments, thereby

significantly reducing unspent balances to near zero

and enhancing financial prudence, efficiency and

transparency. Key Features of SNA-SPARSH Implemen-

tation are asunder:

i. Integration with JJM-IMIS for Scheme-wise
Monitoring: The SNA-SPARSH module of PFMS
shall be integrated with JJM-IMIS to enable
scheme-wise payments and facilitate real-time
monitoring and reporting of financial progress;

ii. Structured Banking Arrangements Based on

Funding Pattern: States/ UTs with different
funding patterns for coverage and Support &
WQM&S components shall maintain separate SLS
and RBI accounts. States/ UTs with uniform funding
patterns shall maintain a single SLS and RBI
account for both components. The department
shall operate a single RBI account for release of the
central share;

Detailed Sustainability Matrix

Drinking Water Sustainability Matrix:

i. Institutional and Service Delivery Sustainability: The institutional framework and governance mechanisms
that enable water supply systems to operate professionally, accountably and sustainably, while delivering

assured service standards to all households:

a) Institutionalise accountability at all levels: State, District, PRI, VWSC/ GP and operators;

b) Assure service delivery and standards.

ii. Source Sustainability: The long-term security of water sources through groundwater recharge, source
protection and integrated water resource management ensuring adequate water availability year-round:

a) Secure water sources through hydrogeology-based planning, recharge structures, water quality surveillance
and infrastructure protection mechanisms.

iii. Financial Sustainability: The ability of water supply schemes to generate sufficient revenue through service
delivery charges to cover operational costs and maintenance, without perpetual subsidy dependence:

a) Ensure financial sustainability by instituting transparent tariff structures and strengthening revenue
collection mechanisms, while effectively communicating the intrinsic value of water services to end-users.

iv. Infrastructure Sustainability: Systematic management of water supply infrastructure assets through digital
registries, preventive maintenance scheduling, lifecycle costing and performance tracking ensuring long asset
life and operational efficiency:

a) Strengthen long-term asset management through asset and inventory management registry, O&M,
preventive maintenance and lifecycle costing.

Support Ecosystem of Sustainability Matrix:

i. Digital Systems: States to progressively adopt integrated digital systems to strengthen planning, monitoring
and accountability of rural water services. Development of GIS based asset registries, service area identifiers,
dashboards and decision support tools can enhance asset visibility, support informed decision making,
improve water quality surveillance and enable transparent service delivery across alllevels;

ii. Governance: States to strengthen governance structures by clarifying institutional roles, enhancing coordina-
tion across departments and aligning water policies with sustainability principles. Empowerment of local
institutions, promotion of regulatory mechanisms for source protection and standardization of asset manage-
ment and O&M practices can support resilient service delivery and longterm drinking water security;

iii. Community Ownership: States to encourage greater community ownership by enabling Gram Panchayats,
village institutions and local youth to participate actively in the management of rural water supply systems.
Structured capacity building programmes, clear operating procedures, local stewardship of water sources and
community engagement initiatives can foster asset ownership and sustainable operations;

iv. Citizen Feedback: States to strengthen citizen centric service assurance by institutionalizing feedback and
grievance redress mechanisms. Regular functionality assessments, transparent tariff communication, service
performance ratings, supply information systems and structured commissioning and handover processes can
improve responsiveness, build trust and support continuous service improvement.

Sujalam Shakti Group

Community-based organisations engaged by VWSC including village level Self Help Groups (SHGs, PACs, etc.) for

supporting safe, reliable and sustainable rural water services shall be referred to as Sujalam Shakti Groups. This will

help align these groups with the objectives of the Jal Jeevan Mission and recognise them as field functionaries for the

Mission. States may issue operational guidelines for these groups. These will preferably be women led community

support system for long-term functionality and sustainability of rural water supply schemes. Under this convergence

framework, identified groups may be oriented and trained to undertake structured roles in coordination with Gram

Panchayats and VWSCs, including:

i. Apply Basic Concepts of Rural Water Supply;

ii. Take uprelevant WOM&S activities at village/ GP level, Conduct Drinking Water Quality Testing using Field Test Kit
(FTK) and Perform Basic Water Disinfection using Chlorine, Bleaching Powder, etc. including:

a. Water quality testing and reporting: Conduct periodic testing of drinking water sources and household supply
using FTKs.and reportresults on designated digital platforms fortimely action;

b. Remedial action support: Coordinate with VWSCs, Gram Panchayats and technical functionaries for prompt
remedial measures in case of contamination or service disruptions;

c. Community surveillance: Support village level vigilance on protection of drinking water sources and infrastruc-
ture from contamination, misuse or damage and promote safe water handling practices.

iii. Support utility tariff collection and community engagement:

a. Awareness and facilitation for service delivery charge: Undertake awareness and mobilisation for timely payment
of service delivery charge and responsible water use for sustainable O&M, IEC & BCC activities etc;

b. Collection of service delivery charge: Where authorised by the Gram Panchayat/VWSC, SHGs may support collec-
tion of service delivery charge and maintenance contributions in a transparent and accountable manner through
digital orreceipt-based systems.

iv. Use Digital, Financial, Communication Skills and Customer Service including grievance redressal at the
Workplace;

v. Implement Source Contamination Prevention and Follow Regional Water Safety Guidelines:

a. Source sustainability: Facilitate community mobilisation for water conservation, recharge and source protection
through convergence with VB-G RAM Gand other local programmes.

Skill Development and LocalO&M Support

The component may include structured skill development of Sujalam Shakti groups to support minor operation and

maintenance activities at the village level. Through appropriate training and resource support systems, selected SHG

members may be trained in:

i. Basic upkeep and cleaning of water supply infrastructure such as overhead tanks, pump houses and surround-
ings;

ii. Support forminor repair and preventive maintenance activities under supervision of VWSC/DTU;

iii, Record-keeping and reporting of functionality issues;

iv. Supportservices forvillage level water system management.

Cluster-based training platforms and resource augmentation mechanisms etc. may be utilised for periodic capacity

building, refresher training and creation of a pool of trained community resource persons. This will not only

strengthen sustainability of water supply systems but also create locallivelihood opportunities for SHG members.

Financial Incentive Framework
To ensure sustained engagement and accountability, States/ UTs may design a suitable financial incentive mecha-
nism. This may include service-based incentives for water quality testing, facilitation of service delivery charge
collection, support for minor O&M activities and performance linked incentives based on functionality, water quality
compliance and community participation indicators.
This convergence will enable creation of a trained, community based strengthened women led local institutions and
ensure sustained delivery of safe and reliable drinking water services in rural areas.
